references.text: Jesus quotes directly from [ref:Ps 31:6|Psalm 31:6]: "Into your hands I commit my spirit." David placed his spirit in God's hands with trust, and Jesus uses the same words at the moment of his death, but adds the address "Father" (Πάτερ), which underscores his unique relationship with God.
Stephen uses almost identical words when he is stoned: "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit" ([ref:Acts 7:59|Acts 7:59]). Stephen follows Jesus' example and commits his spirit to the Lord at his death.

Matthew's parallel account of Jesus' death: "Jesus cried out again with a loud voice and gave up his spirit" ([ref:Matt 27:50|Matthew 27:50]). Here too, the loud cry is described, along with Jesus giving up his spirit.
Mark's parallel account: "But Jesus cried out with a loud voice and breathed his last" ([ref:Mark 15:37|Mark 15:37]).

John's parallel account of Jesus' death: "When Jesus had received the sour wine, he said, 'It is finished!' Then he bowed his head and gave up his spirit" ([ref:John 19:30|John 19:30]). John emphasizes that Jesus actively commits his spirit, in agreement with Luke's account.

Jesus says that no one takes his life from him, but that he lays it down voluntarily ([ref:John 10:17-18|John 10:17-18]). The words "Into your hands I commit my spirit" show that Jesus voluntarily and consciously entrusts his life to the Father.

Peter encourages those who suffer according to God's will to "commit their souls to a faithful Creator" ([ref:1 Pet 4:19|1 Peter 4:19]). The same basic attitude shown by Jesus: placing one's life in God's hands with trust.

Earlier in the crucifixion account, Jesus prays "Father, forgive them" ([ref:Luke 23:34|Luke 23:34]). In both verse 34 and 46, Jesus addresses the Father as "Father," showing his close fellowship with God even in suffering.

In [ref:Ps 22:2|Psalm 22:2], the sufferer cries out "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" – a cry that Matthew and Mark record. Luke instead chooses to recount Jesus' trusting surrender from [ref:Ps 31:6|Psalm 31:6], thus showing a complementary aspect of Jesus' death.
